author: US Bureau of Labor Statistics

kp.k: Lawyer employment increased across every observed vintage
kp.d: The compiled OEWS estimates show wage-and-salary lawyer employment rising from 657,170 in May 2019 to 754,500 in May 2025, a cumulative increase of 97,330 or 14.8%.
qs: Lawyer employment rose in every vintage; cumulative +97,330 (+14.8%).

kp.k: Paralegal employment grew faster than lawyer employment
kp.d: Paralegal and legal-assistant employment increased from 329,870 in May 2019 to 392,880 in May 2025, a cumulative rise of 63,010 or 19.1%, exceeding the percentage growth reported for lawyers.
qs: Paralegal employment rose in every vintage; cumulative +63,010 (+19.1%) May 2019 to May 2025; the largest single-year rise is the latest (+25,660, +7.0%, May 2024 to May 2025).

kp.k: Recent lawyer growth slowed while paralegal growth accelerated
kp.d: The year-over-year calculations show lawyer employment growth declining from approximately 3.5% annually earlier in the series to 0.9% from May 2024 to May 2025. Paralegal growth accelerated over the later vintages and reached 7.0% in the latest step, its highest rate in the series.
qs: Note the shape: lawyer employment growth decelerates across the last two vintages (from roughly +3.5% a year to +0.9%), while paralegal growth accelerates to its fastest rate in the series.

kp.k: Observed trends oppose scaled paralegal AI substitution
kp.d: The document conditionally argues that the observed acceleration in paralegal employment is opposite to the employment signature expected if AI were substituting for paralegals at scale. This is an interpretation of the aggregate series, not a direct measurement of AI adoption or causation.
qs: If AI-driven substitution away from paralegals were operating at scale, the expected signature is the opposite.

kp.k: Lawyer slowdown cannot be attributed specifically to AI
kp.d: Although slower lawyer employment growth could be consistent with an AI-related account, the document emphasizes that hiring caution and demand changes are also possible explanations and that OEWS data cannot distinguish among them.
qs: A deceleration in lawyer growth is consistent with many stories (hiring caution, rate-driven demand shifts, AI among them) and this series cannot distinguish them.

kp.k: Nominal lawyer wages outpaced paralegal wages
kp.d: From May 2019 to May 2025, the reported lawyer median wage increased by 29.9% nominally, compared with 21.6% for paralegals. The lawyer-to-paralegal median-wage ratio consequently widened from 2.38 to 2.54.
qs: Lawyer median wage +29.9% nominal over the series; paralegal median +21.6% — the lawyer:paralegal median ratio widened from 2.38x to 2.54x.

kp.k: OEWS excludes self-employed lawyers and equity partners
kp.d: The estimates cover wage-and-salary workers rather than the entire practising profession. Equity partners, solo practitioners and other self-employed lawyers are excluded, so the document characterizes the figures as a measure of the employed-lawyer market that understates total attorneys in practice.
qs: OEWS estimates are built from a rolling six-panel establishment survey (roughly 1.1 million establishments over three years) and cover wage-and-salary employment only: equity partners, solo practitioners and other self-employed lawyers are outside scope, so the lawyer series understates total attorneys in practice and is best read as the employed-lawyer market.

kp.k: BLS cautions against treating OEWS as time-series data
kp.d: The document identifies important comparability limits: BLS introduced model-based MB3 estimation with the May 2021 vintage, cautions that OEWS was not designed for time-series comparisons, and notes pandemic-era collection effects in the May 2020 and May 2021 panels. Employment figures are rounded and wages are nominal.
qs: BLS moved to model-based (MB3) estimation with the May 2021 vintage and explicitly cautions that OEWS is not designed for time-series comparison; the May 2020 and May 2021 panels also carry pandemic-era collection effects.
Employment is rounded to the nearest 10; wages are nominal.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The document's commentary argues that accelerating paralegal employment growth runs opposite to the expected signature of AI-driven substitution at scale; slowing lawyer employment growth could reflect AI, but the series cannot identify its cause.
pts.d: This is a conditional interpretation of observed employment estimates, not a forecast or a finding that AI has caused or prevented displacement. The document lists hiring caution and rate-driven demand shifts alongside AI as possible explanations for slower lawyer employment growth. The interpretation belongs to the supplied compilation's commentary; the underlying statistics are attributed to BLS, but the text does not establish that BLS made the AI-related interpretation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is national OEWS employment and nominal wage estimates, with computed employment growth rates rather than direct measures of AI adoption or effects.
pts.d: The supplied tables report lawyer employment rising from 657,170 in May 2019 to 754,500 in May 2025, and paralegal/legal assistant employment rising from 329,870 to 392,880. The AI-related interpretation rests principally on the contrasting recent growth rates: lawyer growth slowed to 0.9% in the latest step, while paralegal growth accelerated to 7.0%. The document also reports nominal wage increases and a widening lawyer-to-paralegal median wage ratio, without attributing those wage changes to AI. It describes the estimates as coming from a rolling six-panel establishment survey and acknowledges limits to time-series comparison.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The observations cover May 2019–May 2025 vintages, with the AI-related interpretation focused on recent growth patterns and conditional on substitution operating at scale.
pts.d: No future prediction horizon is supplied. The latest comparison is May 2024 to May 2025. The document cautions that OEWS is not designed for time-series comparison, uses rolling survey panels, changed to model-based estimation in May 2021, and has pandemic-era collection effects in the May 2020 and May 2021 panels. These qualifications accompany the trend interpretation, as does the explicit statement that the series cannot distinguish AI from other explanations.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The relevant populations are US wage-and-salary lawyers and paralegals/legal assistants, not the entire legal profession.
pts.d: The hypothesized AI effect is substitution away from paralegal employment, while AI is also mentioned as one possible contributor to slower employed-lawyer growth. Neither effect is established causally. Equity partners, solo practitioners and other self-employed lawyers are outside the estimates' scope. The document does not isolate entry-level workers, particular firm types, or client outcomes.
